statements.markdown:
In this certificate only,
$b=-w/r$ is a quotient; it is not the derivative $\Phi_{xxx}$ denoted
by $b$ in the unscaled curvature formula. At a fixed positive time
inside the step define

$$
R=r^2,\quad K=rs,\quad b=-w/r,\quad B=b-2v,
\quad L=-rs_{xx},\quad S_1=z+bv-2Rb.
$$

The subscript on $S_1$ distinguishes it from the support set. The
previous comparisons give

$$
R,K,v,B,j,L,S_1\ge0,\qquad b=B+2v\ge0,\qquad Rb^2=w^2,
$$

because $B=-2H$ and $S_1=2rH_x$.
statements.section: 4.4 How the signs make a correction with zero expectation useful

statements.markdown:
For $\mathcal D=r\partial_x$, direct differentiation gives

$$
\mathcal D(R,K,v,b,j)
 =(2Rv,\ 2vK+Rj,\ -Rb,\ -z-bv,\ -jv+Kb-L).
$$

Also $f_x/f=r-s$. Hence
$\mathcal W(F)=\mathcal DF+(v+R-K)F$ satisfies

$$
f\mathcal W(F)=\partial_x(rfF).
$$

This identity does not itself make the integral vanish. The tails give
$r=O(1)$; exponential decay of $v,w,z,b$ and their derivatives;
$s=x/t+O(1)$; $j=1/t+O((1+x)e^{-\kappa x})$; and $K=O(1+x)$.
Every polynomial $F$ in $R,K,v,b,j$ and its differentiated expression
therefore has at most polynomial growth. Meanwhile
$f(t,x)\le C\exp(-x^2/(2t)+C|x|)$. Thus every term used below is
absolutely integrable and $rfF\to0$ at both infinities. Smooth
extension across zero prevents an interior boundary term. Integrating
on $[-A,A]$ and taking $A\to\infty$ now gives
$\mathbb E_f\mathcal W(F)=0$.
statements.section: 4.4 How the signs make a correction with zero expectation useful

The factorisation of the density gives $f_x/f=r-s$. For a suitable
expression $F$ in the shape quantities, define
$$
\mathcal W(F)=r\partial_xF+(v+r^2-rs)F.
$$
Then $f\mathcal W(F)=\partial_x(rfF)$. The smooth extensions
avoid an interior boundary term at zero, and the source's differentiated
Gaussian tail estimates give $rfF\to0$ at both spatial infinities
for the polynomial correction used below. Hence
$\mathbb E_f\mathcal W(F)=0$, where $\mathbb E_f$ denotes integration
against $f(x)\,dx$.

lean.note: The flux derivative, for this one certificate polynomial F2.

statements.markdown:
The operation can be written directly for the positive density $f_t$;
here $f_t'$ means differentiation in the state variable $x$, with $t$ fixed.
For a smooth function $F$ with integrable terms and vanishing boundary
product $Ff_t$,

$$
\mathbb E\!\left[F'(X_t)+F(X_t)\frac{f_t'(X_t)}{f_t(X_t)}\right]
=\int_{\mathbb R}(Ff_t)'(x)\,dx=0.
$$
statements.note: The Lean has the integrated form only for the certificate flux, not for general F.

lean.name: OAI.SKValue.integral_flux_zero
lean.note: Scalar model. A general zero-flux lemma: an integrable derivative of an integrable function integrates to zero.

statements.markdown:
For a small example of this operation, let $Z$ be standard normal and
$F(x)=2x$. Its density has logarithmic derivative $-x$, so
$\mathbb E[2-2Z^2]=0$. Although $2x^2-1$ is negative near zero,
adding that zero-mean correction gives

$$
(2x^2-1)+(2-2x^2)=1.
$$

Hence $\mathbb E[2Z^2-1]=1>0$. The boundary term vanishes because a
polynomial times the Gaussian density tends to zero. This illustrates
how a correction changes the visible sign without changing the
expectation; it supplies none of the SK-specific sign estimates.
statements.note: The example is not in the Lean. Gaussian integration by parts and a general zero-flux lemma are.
